title: Game devs using LLM agents: what keeps going wrong?
author: samnovakfit
selftext:
# [](https://www.reddit.com/r/gamedev/?f=flair_name%3A%22Discussion%22)I’m building a small internal checklist/skill for using LLM coding agents in game dev. What recurring mistakes do you keep seing from tools like Cursor, Claude Code, ChatGPT, Copilot, or custom agents?

# I’m especially interested in mistakes around:

* game architecture
* mobile builds
* UI scaling / safe areas
* asset pipelines
* save/config systems
* ads, IAP, analytics
* ECS
* testing
* performance / memory / rendering

What rules do you now give agents before letting them write code?

comments.author: Ok_Pea_8752
comments.body: im making an online game and i got to make sure it doesnt build the whole game in server/index.ts

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body:
Yes, this is a good one. Agents love putting everything into `server/index.ts` or one giant entry file unless you stop them early.

I’m adding a rule like:

Don’t build the whole game/server in the entry file. `server/index.ts` should only bootstrap the app, load config, register services/routes/systems, and start the server.

Actual logic should be split into modules like networking, rooms/matchmaking, game state, persistence, auth, services, and shared types.  
For online games this matters even more, because server code gets messy fast if architecture is not enforced from the start.

replies.author: GDEmerald
replies.body:
Wouldnt you just do that only in the first prompt? Like once the agent actually has the necessary infrastructure, it wont do that by default. So it is more important, to actually tell them, where stuff should be. Example: Place scenes under /scenes and scene-specifics (like shopComponent) under /scenes/shop/component.tsx

Add a skill for layout. Just telling them "dont do X" without proving an alternative is much worse then to tell them "do Y".



If you are looking for actual skills, the one I am using (that are not custom to my specific project):

\- grill-me (https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/blob/main/skills/productivity/grill-me/SKILL.md)

\- caveman (https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/blob/main/skills/productivity/caveman/SKILL.md)

\- karpathy-guidelines (https://github.com/multica-ai/andrej-karpathy-skills/blob/main/skills/karpathy-guidelines/SKILL.md)

  
The other skills are mainly for discovery (indexing codebase), plan-design, plan-implementation (both written by an gpt and extended with specifics), workspace-tooling (also written by the agent so it does not have to rediscover how to move a file from A to B every single call), testing and packaging.

  
Since you mentioned testing yourself: This is one of the single most important points. Having the option to call "pnpm run verification" for example and checking that every test is clean is huge, so ensure you let your agents build infrastructure for that aswell and reference it in your plan-implementation and plan-design skills.

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
The problem is that past maybe a week of building, any serious project is going to balloon in structure past being easy to simply feed the whole thing back into the AI every time context is refreshed.  Claude, for example, has fresh context *every chat* unless you turn on Memory and make extensive use of Project Files, and even then it will admit itself that it's more of a stop-gap it can sometimes reference and not a true, reliable expansion of context.

Not only will feeding an entire huge project into a new chat every time quickly become untenable as it will cause individual chat context to degrade faster and faster every time, but dear god will it burn tokens like nobody's business.  For long term work on larger projects you *need* to build logistical workflows to compartmentalize pieces of the project that can be handed off to the AI cleanly and focus the work while retaining accuracy.  I'm very partial to having it build a Relationship Map early, and then as an end of session checklist task you have it update the map to reflect today's changes.  That way you have a nice, clean summary doc you can give it at the beginning of every new session so now it *knows* the structure of your project, and that there's an established Namespace for your NPCs, where the classes are, what they do, etc and isn't just making vague contextual assumptions.  When it hits a wall, now it can ask you to upload the applicable script files as needed.

replies.author: GDEmerald
replies.body:
You are absolutely right.

However it also depends on how you develop. I for my part add a feature and then spend the next week ensuring that it blends nicely into the rest of the framework and fixing root issues/extending the framework, where necessary. Obviously this only works, if you have a good structure to begin with, know how things work together and respect SOLID/DRY while KISS (and explicitly tell your agents to respect that during lengthy grill-me sessions).

Most people (like OP I assume), wont have the patience for that. So for them it is most likely "good enough" to have a somewhat manageable structure to begin with.

Obviously the advantage this cyclic workflow brings, is that going wide (aka adding new scenes/ui/dialogues) is fairly easy, but you have to preload a lot of work (go deep immediatly), which once again is not for everyone.

comments.author: Melodic_Charity_1770
comments.body: It depends what engine/platform you're doing. Making a document that is as broad as what OP seems to advise wouldn't be useful - it has to be tailored per project, per game engine. per platform.

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body:
Yeah, I agree with that.

I probably should have been clearer: I don’t think one broad document can solve this by itself. The useful version is probably a base checklist plus project-specific rules for the engine, platform, repo structure, build pipeline, and team conventions.

So for example, the general rule might be “don’t guess engine behavior,” but the actual useful rule needs to point the agent to the specific engine docs/source, project examples, and platform constraints.

That’s a good takeaway: the checklist should start by forcing the agent to identify the exact engine/platform/project context before writing code.

comments.author: miomao10
comments.body: It’s done everything I ever wanted. Sometimes it takes a few tries or bug fixes to get it right or even a creating variants of a feature or idea or ui to find the ideal

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body:
That’s useful to hear too. I think the “create variants and iterate” part is probably one of the strongest use cases.  
Maybe the rule there is: agents are good for exploring options, but the developer still needs to review, pick the direction, and polish the final version.  
I’m adding this as a positive pattern: use agents for fast variants/prototypes, then have strict review rules before anything becomes production code.

comments.author: AverageDrafter
comments.body: When I ask it to build a Godot scene, I have to remind it to build the SCENE - put the actual nodes in the actual scene file, not a script that creates and assembles the scene nodes on run time where it does me no goddamned bit of good for editing it or getting eyes on how its structured.

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body:
This is a really good one. For editor-based engines like Godot/Unity, the agent should not generate everything dynamically in code unless that’s explicitly requested.

I’m adding a rule like: When asked to build a scene/prefab, create the actual editable scene/prefab structure in the engine’s native files, not just a runtime script that assembles nodes/objects on launch.

The result should be inspectable and editable by a human in the editor.

comments.author: sinisoul
comments.body:
I'm building an engine and I have spent a ton of time on:

- Building a pipeline to record and divide up work between agents, each step in the pipeline has a skill and as issues pop up with how they're written they get adjusted.
- Logging, tons and tons of logging. Too much logging. 
- Tracing, tons of tons of internal tracing. 
- MCP architecture + RPC architecture that the agents can freely interact with to debug problems and build features.

The issues I come across are mostly that the agents can only do so much and you need established, well thought out workflows for them to operate within or they will go off the rails. This isn't specific to game development to be honest. 

LLMs respond to "no" by figuring out why and adapting around it. If you don't provide enough "no" signals you will get absolute garbage. This goes for code, assets, anything.

comments.author: ashutrip
comments.body: Do not assume in skills else it assume and over engineers a lot.

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body:
I’m adding this as a core rule: the skill should not let the agent fill gaps with assumptions. It should inspect the project first, follow existing patterns, and make the smallest correct change.

If something is unclear, the agent should say what is unclear instead of inventing architecture, services, ECS systems, folders, tests, or fallback behavior.

A lot of over-engineering seems to come from the agent trying to “complete” missing requirements instead of stopping and verifying them.

comments.author: ffxivthrowaway03
comments.body:
Garbage in, garbage out is still *rule #1*.

I see most people struggle with AI tools in dev (and AI tools in general) because they don't know how to ask for what they want clearly, or even really know *what* they want.

"Build me a login screen for my mobile game in godot" is going to get you absolute unusable crap every single time.

"We're building a login screen for my mobile game GameTitle, it needs four clickable menu items - Start, Load game, Options, Exit that when clicked go to their respective menus.  Attached are the scripts that match the naming convention."  and so on.  
  
Some things I found especially useful on my first day kicking the tires with Claude:

1) Spend almost your *entire* session zero doing no actual game development work.  Write zero lines of code.  Spend this time building *structure* and *ways of working* with the tool.  Pick it's "brain," ask it invasive questions about how it's context window works and where it frequently makes errors for the kind of work you want to do.  You'll build out an entire process (which you will refine over time as you run into gaps and snags) where you specifically spend the first part of every chat feeding the AI established knowledge and context so it doesn't just make wild assumptions about your project.  Like I have it build a relationship map for Unity assets and how they map to the scripts in the project, because *it has no insight into the Unity IDE*.  Well... now it does, it knows what scripts are attached to what objects, the type of objects in the project, etc, because I tell it as one of the first steps in every session.

2)   **Code Gates Are A Must**.  In your ways of working, you should explicitly define that the AI is *not* to start writing code until *you approve the design*.  Claude especially *wants to write code*.  I'd ask it a design question while working out the specifics of a mechanic and it would constantly run off and go "great idea, here's the 200 line script that does it!" when I was not yet committed to that being the final design choice.  Not only did it get very confusing whether it was building a final script I could just dump into the project or if it was iterating on some other work it did that I \*didnt\* import but is now a dependency, it was burning tokens like crazy doing worthless work in Refactor City.  Now we *design*, then confirm, then it writes code that matches the design and I actually understand when I read it by hand.

3) Development by nature is iterative - you make a core function work full of dev placeholders and stub references to things that arent built yet, and then you eventually build that out.  Scope creep is real, and has real project implications.  This is *anathema* to how AI chat context work.  Ask your AI of choice the best way for *it* to help rein that in and it will help develop the process.  Claude specifically has a Projects folder that helps tremendously if you fill it with design docs, summaries of work that you previously did, decision logs, and the latest copy of your codebase.  If you want to be successful, this is a Real Project and you are Designer, Project Manager, and Co-Engineer.  If you just vibe code a bunch of bullshit, you're going to end up with a soggy mess that would have been easier to do by hand.  Know the limitations of the tooling and plan around them, and the more *you* know about software development best practices, CI/CD lifecycle, code review, etc. the more you will get out of these tools.  This is likely **the biggest** divider between people churning out "vibe coded slop" and how we see professional software engineers drastically multiply their productivity while writing less code.  You don't need to go get a CS degree, but dear god their are a million free online courses to learn the basics.  I spent two weeks doing Unity's own free tutorial courses before I ever even created a project file and it was an *invaluable* refresher to my decades old college CS classes.

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body:
This is extremely useful, thanks.

The “garbage in, garbage out” point is probably one of the biggest rules. A vague prompt like “build a login screen” lets the agent invent too much. A useful prompt needs context, constraints, naming conventions, existing scripts, expected behavior, and what should not be changed.

I also really like the “session zero” idea: spend the first session setting up the workflow, project structure, context rules, decision logs, and how the agent should ask before acting instead of jumping straight into code.

The code gate rule is also going into the checklist: no code until the design/approach is approved. First clarify, then propose, then confirm, then implement.

Main takeaways I’m adding:

* give specific requirements, not vague tasks
* feed project context at the start of each session
* maintain design docs / decision logs / project summaries
* make the agent map existing assets/scripts before editing
* require approval before writing code
* prevent scope creep and random refactors
* treat the human as designer / PM / reviewer, not just prompt sender

This is exactly the kind of practical process feedback I was looking for.

comments.author: AgenticGameDev
comments.body: Architecture and testing. I made a tool for the testing and for architecture I do a modular, concrete, facade, router architecture. Works great with agents.

comments.author: NovelFlame_AI
comments.body:
My biggest one is: don't let the agent optimize things it wasn't asked to optimize, I've had cases where a targeted change would turn into a mini refactor because the agent decided the existing implementation wasn't ideal. The code wasn't broken, it just wasn't how the model would've built it from scratch.

Now I'm a big fan of requiring agents to explain what they're changing and why before they touch anything. Half the time you catch the bad assumption before a single line gets written.

comments.author: kkogong07
comments.body:
Really useful thread — would you be willing to share the checklist once it's more fleshed out?  
  
One thing I haven't seen mentioned yet: automated QA as part of the agent workflow. I'm building a web-based game and set up Playwright end-to-end tests specifically so the agent has to run them after every meaningful change. The rule I give it is basically "don't consider a task done until the test suite passes" — it cuts down a lot on the "it works in isolation but broke something else" issues.  
  
There's also a separate layer I think about for runtime, not just dev-time. I'm working on a game with AI NPCs and auto-generated quests, and the checklist problems there are different — things like making sure NPCs don't repeat dialogue they've already said, or that a quest that was already generated doesn't get regenerated again. It's less about code quality and more about state consistency at runtime. Not sure if that's in scope for what you're building, but figured it might be worth distinguishing the two.

replies.author: samnovakfit
replies.body:
Really appreciate this, both points are going in. The automated QA one is a strong addition. I'm adding a rule that the agent treats a task as incomplete until the verification suite passes, not just until the code compiles or the feature works in isolation. Basically: after any meaningful change, run the defined check command (tests, lint, build) and report results before declaring the task done. That catches the works-alone-but-broke-something-else class of bugs that otherwise stays invisible until much later.  
 The dev-time vs runtime split is a distinction I hadn't separated cleanly, and you're right that it's a different problem. Everything in the checklist so far is dev-time: code structure, scope control, asset and scene handling, approval gates. Runtime state consistency (NPCs not repeating dialogue, quests not regenerating, world state staying coherent) is its own layer with its own failure modes, so it probably deserves a separate section rather than being mixed into the code-quality rules. I'll split it that way.     
And yes, happy to share once it's cleaned up. Right now it's a base checklist plus engine and platform specific rules, and I want the structure right before posting so it's actually usable and not just a wall of don'ts.

replies.author: kkogong07
replies.body: Sounds great! I’m looking forward to seeing your checklist. Please make sure to share it when it’s ready haha.

comments.author: eckm4rs
comments.body:
What I didnt see covered or missed when browsing the thread:  
Token efficiency and cost became a big issue lately for me, with antigravity at least.  
  
4 months ago i could progress as much as I wanted on my project ( c# unity and some godot PoCs )any given day as long as i didnt go full vibemind.  
I had to learn how to be token efficient for that with some of the rules already mentioned.  
  
Since last month though I hit the token limits every single day.  
Its not that my codebase exploded, rather the opposite in terms of modularity coupling and readability etc. I did a lot of refactoring and tech debt removal.  
  
The token consumption changed because the models i was using arent available anymore and the system prompts changed.  
What i read about how fable will be billed : its gonna spread to other providers as well.

So my latest rules evolve around having the agent behave context and token aware:  
aka Fighting the system prompt.  
  
My take is that system prompts in general try to boost the products output for wide adaption and new client segments ( aka vibe coders ;D ).  
So in short: The system prompts add a layer of conversation and reasoning based on the assumption that you are not experienced as a developer and need ( a lot of ) assistance.  
  
By testing and reading up I understand the system prompts have extreme differences between the providers, claude code being the king i believe with up to 11 prompt edits / rewrites etc.  
  
My current core "fix antigravity" prompt / skill / rule I run every time goes something like this:

   \* prevent creation of premature implementation plans and tasks that the system prompt asks for.  
   \* Clarification: enforce asking the user back instead of guessing and burning tokens  
\* Clarification has the most potential for saving and productivity imho.  
\* in my experience Claude in general does clarifation quite well.  
   \* enforce "hidden" plans and tasks and chat insights output to be in explicit .md / in git to survive sessions switches and context loss.  
   \* prevent automated test sessions for runtime features that a human validates seconds with 0 tokens.  
   \* apply caveman 😉 and yes: i love the grill-me-with-docs skill .

My next big issue will be:  
Optimizing how to read up on the codebase and current requirements in a new session - in a token efficient manner.

My general rules ( covered already in more detail by previous contributers here )  
\* getting specs clear first and getting them written out in accessible files  
\* at / after implementation phase: stopping wild code bug fix guesswork sessions  
\* various code guards about coding styles, libraries and frameworks etc.   
  
And for your rules I affirm positive "DO THIS" over "DONT do XY".  
Dont´s are endless by definition, you will never cover all.
